patterns_data.top_pattern: CA acute hospital spend is rising across HMO, with a smaller PPO tail
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: Commercial Local Group / CA / ACUTE HOSPITAL
key_driver_codes: Esophagitis, Gastroenteritis and Miscellaneous Digestive Disorders without MCC
Degenerative Nervous System Disorders without MCC
Vaginal Delivery without Sterilization or D&C with CC
patterns_data.pattern_details: CA acute hospital cost pressure is being driven mainly by HMO business, with a smaller PPO contribution. The increase reflects both more claims and higher paid amounts per case, and it is concentrated in a small number of inpatient categories rather than a broad-based hospital trend. This points to a focused provider and case mix issue inside acute hospital spend.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Acute hospital spend is a large, actionable cost lever, and concentrated movement in a few categories can often be addressed faster than a broad utilization trend.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Launch a CA acute hospital review for HMO first, then PPO, combining UM review of admission appropriateness and level of care with reimbursement and network review of the hospitals and contracts tied to the concentrated cases.
patterns_data.validation_reason: A meaningful share of the increase is concentrated in a few cases and low-baseline categories, so confirm claim classification and payment accuracy while pursuing operational action.
evidence_summary: CA HMO acute hospital added about $506K total.
The largest HMO driver was digestive disorders, up about $239K on 3 more claims, with paid per case up about $9.6K.
A single degenerative nervous system case added about $185K in CA HMO acute hospital.
CA PPO acute hospital added another $24K, concentrated at OLYMPIC MEDICAL HOSPITAL with 19 more claims.

Degenerative Nervous System Disorders without MCC
patterns_data.pattern_details: CA inpatient Med/Surg spend increase is coming from a handful of new or rare high-cost admissions, not from broad inpatient growth. The biggest movement sits in digestive disorder and degenerative nervous system cases, each with very high paid amounts per case. This is a classic catastrophic or rare-case pattern that needs case-level review rather than broad policy change.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: A few unusually expensive admissions can materially distort trend and require different action than routine inpatient utilization management.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Send the CA inpatient cases for focused clinical and payment review to confirm severity, coding completeness, stop-loss or transplant-type considerations if relevant, and whether any provider negotiation or case management follow-up is needed.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The increase is driven by very small counts and repeated concentration in rare cases.
evidence_summary: CA IP Med/Surg added about $564K total from 4 cards.
One digestive disorder cluster added about $289K across 3 more claims, with paid per case up about $96K.
A single degenerative nervous system case added about $185K.
All major drivers were flagged as low baseline and highly concentrated.

patterns_data.top_pattern: Not Mapped and unattributed claims are a gating validation issue
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: CA / UNATTRIBUTED / ME / NY / CO across Not Mapped facility and outpatient categories
patterns_data.pattern_details: A meaningful share of the remaining increase sits in Not Mapped facility buckets, Not Mapped outpatient categories, or UNATTRIBUTED segment assignment. That means business users do not yet have reliable provider, facility, or clinical attribution for part of the trend. This should be treated as a gating validation pattern before stronger utilization, reimbursement, or network action is taken on those claims.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: When claims are not mapped cleanly, the organization can misidentify the provider, service type, or policy lever and act on the wrong root cause.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Run a targeted data-quality and claim-mapping audit for Not Mapped and UNATTRIBUTED records, starting with the largest dollars in ME PPO, the outpatient misc and behavioral clusters, and the oncology and lab records tied to named providers.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The contributing groups are explicitly flagged as Not Mapped or UNATTRIBUTED and include unknown-value flags across both operational and clinical findings.
evidence_summary: ME PPO Not Mapped added about $114K even though claims fell by 141, which suggests a classification or unit-cost distortion that needs confirmation.
A concentrated outpatient misc cluster added about $146K in the CA / UNATTRIBUTED segment, led by a 5-claim, roughly $129K increase tied to diagnosis Q812.
UNATTRIBUTED outpatient behavioral health added about $89K, led by F1020 and F4310 in Not Mapped categories.
Smaller Not Mapped lab and oncology increases also appear in CA, NY, and CO, including LABORATORY CORPORATION OF AMERICA, THREE RIVERS DIAGNOSTICS, and OLYMPIC MEDICAL HOSPITAL.

patterns_data.top_pattern: ME PPO physical rehab is showing both volume and unit-cost pressure
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: Commercial Local Group / ME / Physical Rehab / PPO
patterns_data.pattern_details: ME PPO physical rehab spend is increasing through a mix of more claims and higher paid amounts per claim. Unlike many of the smaller outlier patterns, this one has a clearer utilization component and a clearer site-of-care signal. That makes it a practical area for combined UM and provider economics action.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Rehab utilization and reimbursement can move quickly if referral patterns, length of stay, or contracted rates change.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Review ME PPO rehab referrals, admission criteria, and payment terms for physical rehab providers to determine whether the increase is driven more by case growth, intensity, or reimbursement.
evidence_summary: ME PPO Physical Rehab added about $111K total.
Claims increased by 69.
Paid per claim increased by about $1.6K.
The signal is concentrated but materially larger than the smaller one-off segments.

patterns_data.top_pattern: CA maternity spend is being moved by a small number of very high-cost deliveries
key_driver_codes: Vaginal Delivery without Sterilization or D&C with CC
patterns_data.pattern_details: CA maternity spend is not showing a broad delivery surge; it is being driven by a very small number of unusually expensive delivery episodes. One delivery-related diagnosis accounts for most of the increase. This should be handled as a maternity case review and payment accuracy issue rather than a broad obstetric utilization trend.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Maternity episodes often require different clinical and contracting actions than general inpatient trends, so separating them avoids a diluted response.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Perform case-level maternity review on the delivery episodes behind the increase, confirming clinical severity, reimbursement accuracy, and whether any maternity case-management intervention is warranted.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The increase is concentrated in one to two delivery episodes with low baseline volume.
evidence_summary: CA IP OB Dlvry/Well NB added about $99K total.
One delivery diagnosis, O368130, added about $88K from a single claim.
A second diagnosis, O480, added about $11K from one claim.
The pattern is concentrated in vaginal delivery with CC rather than broad maternity growth.

patterns_data.pattern_details: Beyond CA and ME, several smaller state and product combinations show acute hospital cost increases that are real but highly concentrated. These are mostly one-provider or one-DRG outliers, so they should be managed as emerging pockets of pressure rather than broad market shifts. The common business lever is targeted provider and claim review by product and facility.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Smaller pockets of concentrated acute hospital spend can become recurring issues if they are not addressed early at the provider or contract level.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Create a small-market acute hospital watchlist for OH, MO, CO, GA, IN, and WI and route each segment to network and UM teams for targeted provider-level review instead of a broad policy change.
patterns_data.validation_reason: Most contributing groups are low-volume and concentrated in one provider or one DRG.
evidence_summary: These smaller acute hospital segments add up to about $159K.
OH HMO acute hospital added about $52K, concentrated at FAIRFIELD MEDICAL CENTER with 4 more claims.
MO PPO acute hospital added about $49K from a single degenerative nervous system case.
CO and GA EPO acute hospital added about $43K combined, led by WELLSTAR COBB MEDICAL CENTER and biliary tract cases.

patterns_data.pattern_details: This multi-state inpatient Med/Surg pattern is made up of isolated high-cost admissions across several states, not a recurring clinical trend in one market. Sepsis, poisoning, biliary, and hip-fracture-related admissions are the main drivers. The right response is selective case review, not a broad utilization intervention.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Rare inpatient outliers can distort trend and may point to one-time severity, coding, or payment issues that need case-level handling.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Route the identified inpatient cases for clinical and payment review, with special attention to the providers and diagnoses driving the largest single-admission increases.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The pattern is built from one-claim and low-volume admissions across multiple states.
evidence_summary: CO, GA, IN, and OH IP Med/Surg added about $98K total.
A sepsis-related admission at FAIRFIELD MEDICAL CENTER added about $52K.
A poisoning-related admission at WELLSTAR COBB MEDICAL CENTER added about $27K.
The remaining increase came from single-case biliary and hip-fracture admissions.
